newsletters.title: Context Engineering Is Knowing When to Start Over
newsletters.content:
Old instructions and earlier mistakes can derail your AI chats. Here’s how to reset without losing useful work.  ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌
https://every.?ev_audience=free

Also True for Humans

https://every.?ev_audience=free


CONTEXT ENGINEERING IS KNOWING WHEN TO START OVER https://every.?ev_audience=free


OLD INSTRUCTIONS AND EARLIER MISTAKES CAN DERAIL YOUR AI CHATS. HERE’S HOW TO RESET WITHOUT LOSING USEFUL WORK. https://every.?ev_audience=free

by Mike Taylor https://every.?ev_audience=free

Midjourney/Every illustration.

Was this newsletter forwarded to you? Sign up https://every.?ev_audience=free to get it in your inbox.



----------------------------------------



The people I work with know I keep Claude’s memory turned off. The same goes for ChatGPT. I’ve written before about why https://every.?ev_audience=free: Memory can be useful, but it can also bring old preferences and irrelevant instructions into a conversation where they don’t belong.

Turning memory off doesn’t entirely solve the problem. Even within a single thread, context can accumulate in ways that make the model’s responses worse—a problem known as context rot. It might keep following instructions you’ve moved on from, build on an earlier mistake, or overlook a crucial detail buried in the conversation.

That’s why I start a fresh thread for every task. If the task changes, I open a new chat—even if it’s for the same project I was working on five minutes ago.

In my forthcoming book, Context Engineering with DSPy https://every.?ev_audience=free, I explore the seven ways in which context goes wrong and what to do about it. newsletters.title: How Codex Happened
newsletters.content:
Inside OpenAI’s comeback in coding, from a failed launch to the app that took over ChatGPT  ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌
https://every.?ev_audience=free


HOW CODEX HAPPENED https://every.?ev_audience=free


INSIDE OPENAI’S COMEBACK IN CODING, FROM A FAILED LAUNCH TO THE APP THAT TOOK OVER CHATGPT https://every.?ev_audience=free

by Dan Shipper https://every.?ev_audience=free

Midjourney/Photoshop/Every illustration.

This is a free preview of a subscribers-only post.

Was this newsletter forwarded to you? Sign up https://every.?ev_audience=free to get it in your inbox.



----------------------------------------



Codex is one of the most important untold stories in the history of technology.

A year ago, OpenAI’s coding effort looked lost in the wilderness:

 * Codex Cloud had flopped.
 * Their $3 billion Windsurf deal fell apart.
 * Claude Code was running away with the market.

Less than 12 months later, a tiny team in the “backwaters” of OpenAI built an app that grew to more than 40 million users, swallowed ChatGPT from the inside, and remade the entire company.

I had a front-row seat to the whole arc—from a conference room in their office the night before GPT-5 launched to the day Codex took over ChatGPT—and spent months interviewing the people who made it happen, including OpenAI’s Greg Brockman and Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux. It’s a wild story about what it takes to build when the frontier is moving beneath your feet:

Read ‘How Codex Happened’ https://every.?ev_audience=free

Your free Every account includes 10 prompts for applying lessons from the story to your own work and the story as a PDF.

The story is also completely agent-native. Paid members get the full transcripts of all six of my interviews with OpenAI insiders, and a live session with me tomorrow about how we reported and wrote the story with Codex and what I learned about how OpenAI came back.

Nearly every startup pivots eventually, says Matt Hartman, founder of Factorial Capital, so he backs founders with a technical edge and hard-earned insights who are best equipped to navigate a change in markets. On this week’s episode of The Every Podcast, he tells Natalia Quintero https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0Ijoi8J-?ev_audience=free how he finds those founders and why vibe coding his own app gave him new respect for paying for software. Plus: a field report from a 28-person agricultural technology startup that runs on agents in Slack, Becky Isjwara on using the Every Agent as her onboarding buddy, and seven new Thesis Statements.

WHY TECHNICAL FOUNDERS WIN WHEN STARTUPS PIVOT

Matt Hartman, who was part of the Betaworks team that wrote its first check, sees a lesson in that transformation: Back technical founders who can “move with where the world goes.”
